nodes.name: Nonlinear Fokker--Planck equation (1.1)
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} \barr{ll} u_t-\Delta\beta(u)+{\rm div}(b(x,u)u)=0\mbox{ in }\cald'((0,\9)\times\rr^d),\vsp u(0,x)=u_0(x), \earr\end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The nonlinear Fokker--Planck Cauchy problem $u_t-\Delta\beta(u)+{\rm div}(b(x,u)u)=0$ with initial datum $u_0$.

nodes.name: Hypothesis (i): strong monotonicity of $\beta$
nodes.statement: \item[(i)] {\it$\beta(0)=0$, $\b\in C^1(\rr)$, and \begin{equation} \g_0|r_1-r_2|^2\le(\b(r_1)-\b(r_2))(r_1-r_2),\ r_1,r_2\in\rr, \end{equation} where $0<\g_0<\9.$ }
nodes.statement_short: $\beta$ is $C^1$, vanishes at $0$, and is strongly monotone with constant $\g_0>0$.

nodes.name: Hypothesis (ii): regularity and boundedness of the drift $b$
nodes.statement: \item[(ii)] $b\in C_b(\mathbb R^{d+1}; \rrd)$, $b(x, \cdot) \in C^1(\rrd; \rrd)$ $ \forall x\in\rrd$ {\it such that} $$\mbox{$\sup\{|b^i_r(x,r)|;x\in\rrd,i=1,2,$ $|r|\le M\}\le C_M,$ $\ff M>0.$}$$
nodes.statement_short: $b$ is bounded continuous, $C^1$ in the state variable, with locally uniformly bounded $r$-derivatives.

nodes.name: Hypothesis (ii'): $b(x,0)=0$ and bounded $x$-gradient
nodes.statement: \item[(ii')] $b(x,0)=0$ $\forall x\in\rrd$, $b \in C^1(\mathbb R^{d+1}; \rrd) $ {\it and for $$\delta(r):=\sup\{|b_x(x,r)|;\ x\in\rrd\},$$we have} $\delta\in C_b(\rr).$
nodes.statement_short: $b$ vanishes at $r=0$, is $C^1$, and $\delta(r)=\sup_x|b_x(x,r)|$ is bounded continuous.

nodes.name: Notation $b^*(x,u)=b(x,u)u$
nodes.statement: (In the following, we shall use the notation $b^*(x,u)=b(x,u)u.$)

nodes.name: Existence of a mild solution to the nonlinear Fokker--Planck equation
nodes.statement: In \cite{1} it was proved, in particular, that, if (i)--(ii) hold and, in addition, for $\Phi(u)\equiv\frac{\beta(u)}u,$ $u\in\rr,$ we have $\Phi\in C^2(\rr)$, then there is a mild solution $u\in C([0,\9);L^1(\rr^d))$ for each $u_0\in L^1(\rr^d)$.
nodes.statement_short: Under (i)--(ii) and $\Phi=\beta(u)/u\in C^2$, a mild solution exists in $C([0,\infty);L^1)$ for every $L^1$ datum.
conclusions: there is a mild solution $u\in C([0,\9);L^1(\rr^d))$ for each $u_0\in L^1(\rr^d)$

nodes.name: Mild solution
nodes.statement: The mild solution $u$ is defined~as $$u(t)=\lim_{h\to0}u_h(t)\mbox{ in }L^1(\rr^d),\ \ff t\ge0,$$where \begin{equation} \barr{l} u_h(t)=u^i_h\mbox{ for }t\in[ih,(i+h)h],\ i=0,1,...,Nh=T,\vsp u^{i+1}_h-h\D\b(u^{i+1}_h)+h\,{\rm div}(b(x,u^{i+1}_h)u^{i+1}_h)=u^i_h\mbox{ in }\cald'(\rr^d),\\\hfill i=0,1,...,\vsp u^0_h=u_0.\earr \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Limit in $L^1$ of the piecewise-constant implicit Euler scheme $u^{i+1}_h-h\Delta\beta(u^{i+1}_h)+h\,{\rm div}(b^*)=u^i_h$.

nodes.name: Nonexpansive semigroup $S(t)$ generated by the Fokker--Planck flow
nodes.statement: Moreover, $S(t)u_0=u(t),\ t\ge0,$ is a strongly continuous semigroup of nonexpansive mappings in $L^1(\rrd)$.
conclusions: is a strongly continuous semigroup of nonexpansive mappings in $L^1(\rrd)$

nodes.name: McKean--Vlasov SDE (1.7)
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} dX(t)=b(X(t),u(t,X(t)))dt+\frac1{\sqrt{2}}\(\frac{\b(u(t,X(t))}{u(t,X(t))}\)^{\frac12}dW(t). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The McKean--Vlasov SDE whose diffusion coefficient is $(\beta(u)/u)^{1/2}$ evaluated at the marginal density.

nodes.name: Scalar product $\<\cdot,\cdot\>_{-1}$ and norm $|\cdot|_{-1}$ on $H^{-1}$
nodes.statement: The~scalar product $\<\cdot,\cdot\>_{-1}$ on $H\1$ is taken~as \begin{equation} \<u,v\>_{-1}=\<(I-\D)\1u,v\>_2,\ \ff u,v\in H\1 \end{equation}with the corresponding norm \begin{equation} |u|_{-1}=(\<u,u\>_{-1})^{\frac12},\ u\in H\1. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Theorem 2.1 (uniqueness of distributional solutions)
nodes.statement: Let $T>0$ and let conditions {\rm(i)--(ii)} on $\beta$ and $b$ hold. For each $u_0\in L^\9\cap L^1$, the \FP\ equation \eqref{e1.1} has at most one distributional solution \begin{equation} u\in L^1((0,T);L^1)\cap L^\9((0,T)\times\rrd). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Under (i)--(ii), the nonlinear Fokker--Planck equation has at most one bounded distributional solution.
conclusions: the \FP\ equation \eqref{e1.1} has at most one distributional solution \begin{equation} u\in L^1((0,T);L^1)\cap L^\9((0,T)\times\rrd). \end{equation}

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2.1
nodes.statement: Let $u_1,u_2\in L^1(0,T;L^1)\cap L^\9((0,T)\times\rrd)$ be two distributional solutions to \eqref{e1.1} and let $u=u_1-u_2.$ We have \begin{equation} \barr{l} u_t-\D(\b(u_1)-\b(u_2))+{\rm div}(b^*(x,u_1)-b^*(x,u_2))=0\\\hfill\mbox{ in }\cald'((0,\9)\times\rrd)\vsp u(0,x)=0.\earr \end{equation} (Here, $b^*(x,r)=b(x,r)r,\ \ff x\in\rrd,\ r\in\rr.$) It should be mentioned that, by (i), (ii), it follows that $u_i,\beta(u_i), b^*(\cdot, u_i)\in L^2((0,T);L^2),$ $i=1,2$, and, therefore, $u\in W^{1,2}([0,T];H^{-2}).$ Consider the operator $\Gamma:H\1\to H^1$ defined by $$\Gamma u=(1-\D)^{-1}u,\ u\in H\1(\rrd)$$and note that $\Gamma$ is an isomorphism of $H\1$ onto $H^1$ and $\Gamma\in L(H^{-2},L^2).$ Since $u_i\in L^2(0,T;L^2),$ $i=1,2,$ it follows that $y=\Gamma u\in L^2(0,T;H^2)\cap W^{1,2}([0,T];L^2)$ and so, by~\eqref{e2.1}, we have \begin{equation} \barr{l} \dd\frac{dy}{dt}-\Gamma\D(\b(u_1)-\b(u_2))+\Gamma\,{\rm div}(b^*(x,u_1)-b^*(x,u_2))=0,\\\hfill\mbox{ a.e. }t\in(0,T),\\ y(0)=0,\earr \end{equation} where $\frac{dy}{dt}\in L^2(0,T;L^2).$ (We note that here $\frac{dy}{dt}$ is taken in the sense of $L^2$-valued vectorial distributions on $(0,T)$ and so $y:[0,T]\to L^2$ is absolutely continuous.) Assume first that, in addition, \begin{equation} u\in L^2(0,T;H^1);\ u\in W^{1,2}([0,T];H^{-1}). \end{equation} Now, we take the scalar product in $L^2$ of \eqref{e2.2} with $u=u_1-u_2$. Taking into account that $$\<\frac{du}{dt}\,(t),u(t)\>_{-1}=\frac12\ \frac d{dt}\,|u(t)|^2_{-1}, \mbox{ a.e. }t\in(0,T),$$we get, by \eqref{e2.2} that $$\barr{l} \dd\frac 12\ \frac d{dt}\,|u(t)|^2_{-1}+\<\b(u_1)-\b(u_2),u_1-u_2\>_2 =\<\Gamma(\b(u_1)-\b(u_2)),u_1-u_2\>_2\vsp \qquad-\<\Gamma\,{\rm div}((b^*(x,u_1)-b^*(x,u_2)),u_1-u_2\>_2,\ \mbox{a.e. }t\in(0,T).\earr$$ By \eqref{e1.2}, this yields for a.e.~$t\in(0,T)$ \begin{equation} \barr{r} \dd\frac12\ \frac d{dt}\,|u(t)|^2_{-1}+\g_0|u(t)|^2_2 \le\<\b(u_1(t))-\b(u_2(t)),u_1(t)-u_2(t)\>_{-1}\vsp \qquad-\<{\rm div}(b^*(x,u_1(t))-b^*(x,u_2(t))),u_1-u_2\>_{-1}.\earr \end{equation} We note that \begin{equation} |\Gamma f|_2\le|f|_2,\ \ff f\in L^2. \end{equation} We also have \begin{equation} |{\rm div}\,F|_{-1}\le2|F|_2,\ \ff F\in (L^2)^d. \end{equation}This yields \begin{equation} \barr{ll} |\<\b(u_1)-\b(u_2),u_1-u_2\>_{-1}| \le|\b(u_1)-\b(u_2)|_{2}|u|_{-1} \le\b_M|u|_2|u|_{-1} \earr\end{equation}and \begin{equation} \barr{l} \left|\<{\rm div}\ (b^*(x,u_1)-b^*(x,u_2)),u_1-u_2\>_{-1}\right|\vsp \qquad\le 2|b^*(x,u_1)-b^*(x,u_2)|_2|u_1-u_2|_{-1}\vsp \qquad\le2(|b|_\9+b_M|u_1|_\9)|u|_2|u|_{-1}, \earr \end{equation} where $M=\max\{|u_1|_\9,|u_2|_\9)$ and $$\barr{lcl} \b_M&=&\dd\sup\{\b'(r);\ |r|\le M\},\vsp b_M&=&\dd\sup\left\{\frac{|b(x,u_1)-b(x,u_2)|}{|r_1-r_2|};\ x\in\rrd,\ |r_1|,|r_2|<M\right\}\vsp&\le& \sup\{|b_r(x,r)|;|r|\le M,\ x\in\rrd\} < \infty \earr$$ by (ii). By \eqref{e2.3}--\eqref{e2.7}, we get $$\barr{r} \dd\frac12\ \frac d{dt}\,|u(t)|^2_{-1}+\g_0|u(t)|^2_{2} \le(\b_M+2(|b|_\9+b_M|u_1|_\9) |u(t)|^{}_2|u(t)|^{}_{-1},\\\hfill\mbox{a.e. }t\in(0,T).\earr$$ This yields $$\frac d{dt}\,|u(t)|^2_{-1}\le C|u(t)|^2_{-1},\mbox{ a.e. }t\in(0,T).$$Since $u:[0,T]\to H^{-1}$ is absolutely continuous and narrowly continuous, we infer that $|u(t)|_{-1}=0$, $\ff t\in[0,T]$, and so $u\equiv0$, as claimed.
nodes.statement_short: $H^{-1}$ energy estimate on the difference $u_1-u_2$, then Gronwall gives $|u(t)|_{-1}\equiv0$.

nodes.name: The isomorphism $\Gamma=(1-\Delta)^{-1}$
nodes.statement: Consider the operator $\Gamma:H\1\to H^1$ defined by $$\Gamma u=(1-\D)^{-1}u,\ u\in H\1(\rrd)$$and note that $\Gamma$ is an isomorphism of $H\1$ onto $H^1$ and $\Gamma\in L(H^{-2},L^2).$

nodes.name: Contraction bound $|\Gamma f|_2\le|f|_2$ (2.4)
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} |\Gamma f|_2\le|f|_2,\ \ff f\in L^2. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Divergence bound $|{\rm div}\,F|_{-1}\le2|F|_2$ (2.5)
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} |{\rm div}\,F|_{-1}\le2|F|_2,\ \ff F\in (L^2)^d. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Proposition 2.3 ($L^\infty$ bound on the mild solution)
nodes.statement: Assume that {\rm (i), (ii), (ii')} hold, and that, for $\Phi(u)\equiv\frac{\beta(u)}u$, \begin{itemize} \item[{\rm(iii)}] $\Phi\in C^2(\rrd).$ \end{itemize} Then, for each $u_0\in L^1\cap L^\9$, the mild solution $u$ to \eqref{e1.1} satisfies also \begin{equation} u\in L^\9((0,T)\times\rrd),\ \ff T>0. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Under (i), (ii), (ii'), (iii) the mild solution stays in $L^\infty((0,T)\times\mathbb{R}^d)$ for every $T$.
conclusions: the mild solution $u$ to \eqref{e1.1} satisfies also \begin{equation} u\in L^\9((0,T)\times\rrd),\ \ff T>0. \end{equation}

nodes.statement_short: Combining Theorem 2.1 and Proposition 2.3: the Fokker--Planck equation is well posed in the distributional class.

nodes.statement: {\bf(Linearized uniqueness)} Under hypotheses {\rm(i)--(ii)}, for each $v_0\in L^1\cap L^\9$ and $T>0$, equation \eqref{e3.1} has at most one distributional solution $v\in L^{1}([0,T];L^1)\cap L^\9((0,T)\times\rrd).$

conclusions: equation \eqref{e3.1} has at most one distributional solution $v\in L^{1}([0,T];L^1)\cap L^\9((0,T)\times\rrd).$

nodes.name: Proof of the linearized uniqueness theorem
nodes.statement: We shall proceed as in the proof of Theorem \ref{t1}. Namely, we set $v_1-v_2=v$ for two solutions $v_1,v_2$ of \eqref{e3.2} By a similar argument as in the proof of Theorem \ref{t1}, we may assume that $v$ satisfies \eqref{add-e6}. Then we get \begin{equation} \barr{l} v_t-\D(\Psi v)+{\rm div}(b(x,u)v)=0,\mbox{ a.e. }t\in(0,T),\vsp v(0)=0.\earr \end{equation} For $y=\Gamma v$, we get \begin{equation} \barr{l} \dd\frac d{dt}\ y-\Gamma\D(\Psi v)+\Gamma\ {\rm div}(b(x,u)v)=0\vsp y(0)=0\earr \end{equation} and multiplying scalarly in $L^2$ with $v$, as above we get that \begin{equation} \barr{l} \dd\frac12\ \frac d{dt}\ |v(t)|^2_{-1}+\g_0|v(t)|^2_2 \le(|\Psi|_\9+|b|_\9)|v(t)|^{}_2|v(t)|^{}_{-1},\mbox{ a.e. }t\in(0,T).\earr \end{equation} This yields $$\frac d{dt}\ |v(t)|^2_{-1}\le|v(t)|^2_{-1}\mbox{ a.e. }t\in(0,T),$$ and, therefore, $v\equiv0$, as claimed.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.1
nodes.statement: By It\^o's formula, both $u$ and $\wt u$ satisfy the (nonlinear) \FP\ equation \eqref{e1.1} in the sense of Schwartz distributions. Hence, by Theorem \ref{t1}, $u=\wt u$. Furthermore, again by It\^o's formula, $\mathbb{P}\circ X\1$ and $\mathbb{P}\circ\wt X\1$ satisfy the martingale problem with the initial condition $u_0dx$ for the linear Komogorov operator $$L_u:=\Phi(u)\D+b(\cdot,u)\cdot\nabla,$$where $\Phi(u)=\frac{\b(u)}u,$ $u\in\rr.$ Hence, by Theorem \ref{t5}, the assertion follows by Lemma 2.12 in \cite{4}. Here, for $s\in[0,T]$, the set $\mathcal{R}_{[s,T]}$, which appears in that lemma, is chosen to be the set of all narrowly continuous, probability measure-valued solutions of \eqref{e3.1} having for each $t\in[s,T]$ a density \mbox{$v(t,\cdot)\in L^\9$} with respect to Lebesgue measure such that \mbox{$v\in L^\9((0,T)\times\rrd).$}

nodes.name: Set up the difference of two solutions
nodes.statement: Let $u_1,u_2\in L^1(0,T;L^1)\cap L^\9((0,T)\times\rrd)$ be two distributional solutions to \eqref{e1.1} and let $u=u_1-u_2.$ We have \begin{equation} \barr{l} u_t-\D(\b(u_1)-\b(u_2))+{\rm div}(b^*(x,u_1)-b^*(x,u_2))=0\\\hfill\mbox{ in }\cald'((0,\9)\times\rrd)\vsp u(0,x)=0.\earr \end{equation} (Here, $b^*(x,r)=b(x,r)r,\ \ff x\in\rrd,\ r\in\rr.$)

nodes.statement_short: Hypotheses (i)--(ii) give $L^2$ integrability of $u_i,\beta(u_i),b^*$, hence $u\in W^{1,2}([0,T];H^{-2})$.

nodes.name: Introduce the resolvent isomorphism $\Gamma$ and rewrite the equation
nodes.statement: Consider the operator $\Gamma:H\1\to H^1$ defined by $$\Gamma u=(1-\D)^{-1}u,\ u\in H\1(\rrd)$$and note that $\Gamma$ is an isomorphism of $H\1$ onto $H^1$ and $\Gamma\in L(H^{-2},L^2).$ Since $u_i\in L^2(0,T;L^2),$ $i=1,2,$ it follows that $y=\Gamma u\in L^2(0,T;H^2)\cap W^{1,2}([0,T];L^2)$ and so, by~\eqref{e2.1}, we have \begin{equation} \barr{l} \dd\frac{dy}{dt}-\Gamma\D(\b(u_1)-\b(u_2))+\Gamma\,{\rm div}(b^*(x,u_1)-b^*(x,u_2))=0,\\\hfill\mbox{ a.e. }t\in(0,T),\\ y(0)=0,\earr \end{equation} where $\frac{dy}{dt}\in L^2(0,T;L^2).$ (We note that here $\frac{dy}{dt}$ is taken in the sense of $L^2$-valued vectorial distributions on $(0,T)$ and so $y:[0,T]\to L^2$ is absolutely continuous.)
nodes.statement_short: Set $y=\Gamma u$ with $\Gamma=(1-\Delta)^{-1}$, turning (2.1) into the absolutely continuous $L^2$-valued equation (2.2).

nodes.statement: Assume first that, in addition, \begin{equation} u\in L^2(0,T;H^1);\ u\in W^{1,2}([0,T];H^{-1}). \end{equation}

nodes.statement: Now, we take the scalar product in $L^2$ of \eqref{e2.2} with $u=u_1-u_2$. Taking into account that $$\<\frac{du}{dt}\,(t),u(t)\>_{-1}=\frac12\ \frac d{dt}\,|u(t)|^2_{-1}, \mbox{ a.e. }t\in(0,T),$$we get, by \eqref{e2.2} that $$\barr{l} \dd\frac 12\ \frac d{dt}\,|u(t)|^2_{-1}+\<\b(u_1)-\b(u_2),u_1-u_2\>_2 =\<\Gamma(\b(u_1)-\b(u_2)),u_1-u_2\>_2\vsp \qquad-\<\Gamma\,{\rm div}((b^*(x,u_1)-b^*(x,u_2)),u_1-u_2\>_2,\ \mbox{a.e. }t\in(0,T).\earr$$ By \eqref{e1.2}, this yields for a.e.~$t\in(0,T)$ \begin{equation} \barr{r} \dd\frac12\ \frac d{dt}\,|u(t)|^2_{-1}+\g_0|u(t)|^2_2 \le\<\b(u_1(t))-\b(u_2(t)),u_1(t)-u_2(t)\>_{-1}\vsp \qquad-\<{\rm div}(b^*(x,u_1(t))-b^*(x,u_2(t))),u_1-u_2\>_{-1}.\earr \end{equation}
